Lessons.Title: Equal Groups of Unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: You will interpret and relate descriptions, drawings, and multiplication expressions that represent equal groups of unit fractions.
Key idea: Whole-number groups of unit fractions form a product equal to repeated addition of the same fractional amount.
How to reason: Multiply the number of groups by the fractional amount in each group; preserve the fraction unit.
Source-inspired opening: Warm-up: How Many Do You See: Oranges (10 minutes). Use the teacher-provided mathematical representations and explain how different valid answers arise.

First-party discussion supports clear strategies and comparisons, while original drawings and classroom materials are teacher-led.

Activity 2: What Could It Mean? (15 minutes): apply the learning goal to quantities such as \(8 \times \frac{1}{2}\), \(7 \times \frac {1}{5}\). First-party discussion supports clear strategies and comparisons, while original drawings and classroom materials are teacher-led.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal Groups of Unit Fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Whole-number groups of unit fractions form a product equal to repeated addition of the same fractional amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply the number of groups by the fractional amount in each group; preserve the fraction unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five plates each contain 1/2 of an orange. What total fractional orange amount is represented?

KeyConcepts.Title: Same whole and accurate representation
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read the original task conditions before performing arithmetic.
KeyConcepts.Example: Check the work with the rational equality or inequality.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated addition keeps the unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Whole-number multiplication counts copies of the same fractional unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: n groups of 1/d gives n/d of the same whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independently authored source-aligned model
WorkedExamples.Question: Five plates each contain 1/2 of an orange. What total fractional orange amount is represented?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the number of groups by the fractional amount in each group; preserve the fraction unit.
Steps: Add 1/2 five times, or multiply 5 by 1/2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exact rational calculation confirmed; source example not copied.

WorkedExamples.Title: Edulytics model: three quarters by equal groups
WorkedExamples.Question: Three plates each hold 1/4 of an orange. What is the total?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use repeated addition and a whole partitioned in fourths.
Steps: Each plate contributes one fourth of an equally sized orange.
WorkedExamples.Check: The physical representation remains subject to teacher review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Edulytics model: eight eighths make one whole
WorkedExamples.Question: Eight equal groups each contain 1/8 of a unit. How many wholes is that?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count eighth-sized pieces without changing the partition size.
Steps: A complete whole is divided into eight equal parts.
Eight groups each contribute one of those 1/8 pieces.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exact rational equality, using one consistent whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying a fraction denominator by the number of groups instead of counting unit pieces.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It does not preserve the intended mathematical relationship or original task condition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply the number of groups by the fractional amount in each group; preserve the fraction unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing the denominator when counting more equal groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Three quarter-sized pieces are still quarters of one same-sized whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep denominator 4 and count 3 unit pieces to get 3/4.
